Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Health | National JAY Foundation urges post-discharge care for premature babies and their mothers in Ghana Source : Anneta Adams 17 November 2026 5:15pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
For many families, the arrival of a baby is a moment of joy. But when a child is born prematurely, that excitement can quickly give way to fear, uncertainty and emotional distress.
Mothers may have to cope with an unexpected delivery, separation from their newborns and the anxiety of watching them receive specialised care in incubators or neonatal intensive care units.
The challenges often continue after discharge, with the cost of treatment, repeated hospital visits and the demands of caring for a fragile newborn placing additional pressure on families.
For Lamisi, a mother who delivered her baby prematurely at eight months, the experience began with what she expected to be a routine antenatal visit.
She said she was unexpectedly informed that her baby had to be delivered immediately.
“I didn't even get to know. I just went for my routine checks and I was being told that the baby had to be removed. I wasn't informed prior to it. It was an emergency delivery,” she recalled.
The delivery marked the beginning of an emotionally difficult period. While other mothers in the hospital breastfed and carried their newborns, Lamisi had to watch hers remain in an incubator.
“You're in a hospital and you're seeing other mothers carrying their babies, breastfeeding, and yours is in a box. You're separated from your baby. Emotionally, it wasn't the best then,” she said.
She described the experience as both emotionally and financially draining, saying it made her appreciate the importance of having people to rely on during such a difficult period.
“It was very demanding, emotionally and financially draining. We needed a support system and, by God's grace, we got one,” she added.
Lamisi's experience reflects the difficulties some families face when navigating premature birth, particularly when the demands of caring for a newborn continue long after delivery.
The JAY Foundation says it is working to address some of these challenges by improving the survival of premature babies and supporting their mothers.
Its founder, Naa Kuorkor Mayne-Eghan, believes more attention must be paid to the period after babies leave hospital, when families may still need medical guidance and practical assistance.
She is calling on government to strengthen post-discharge care by ensuring that community health nurses and home care nurses visit premature babies and their mothers for at least three months after discharge.
According to her, regular home visits would help families manage the challenges of caring for premature babies and provide guidance during a critical stage of their development.
The Foundation says it works with hospitals across Ghana but needs greater public support to extend its reach and improve outcomes for premature babies.
Mayne-Eghan has also encouraged mothers who deliver prematurely not to suffer in silence or feel ashamed to ask for assistance, stressing that support is available and they should reach out when they need it.
For mothers like Lamisi, delivering a premature baby is only the beginning of a demanding journey.
The experience can involve prolonged hospital care, separation from a newborn, financial strain and the uncertainty of managing the baby's needs after returning home.
The JAY Foundation believes that stronger support systems, including sustained medical guidance and practical assistance after discharge, could help ease the burden on families and improve the chances of survival for premature babies.
